messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus was forty-six when the world narrowed. On a Tuesday evening in March, he had been driving home from his design firm in Portland, taking the back roads through Gresham as he always did, when he saw the police cruiser in his mirror. His hands had been steady on the wheel—he had done nothing wrong—but something in the way the lights came on made his stomach drop. The officer who approached had been agitated, speaking in clipped sentences, and within moments had opened Marcus's door, yanked him from the driver's seat, and slammed him against the hood. There had been no warning, no clear explanation. Marcus's face had been pressed into the metal, his arm twisted behind him, and for the first time in his life he felt utterly powerless, utterly at the mercy of someone whose authority was absolute. The officer had discovered nothing—no warrant, no outstanding issue, nothing—but by then Marcus's nervous system had already learned a terrible lesson. When the officer finally let him go with a curt apology, Marcus had driven home in silence, his entire body trembling.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus returned to work, but something had fractured. He had built a careful life: twenty-two years married to his wife Elena, a respected position designing websites and branding materials for tech startups, a quiet routine of morning coffee and evening walks. Now, each time he heard a siren or saw a police car, his chest would tighten and his mind would flood with the image of that hood, the pressure on his face, the absolute certainty that something terrible was happening. The sight of a bruise on a colleague's arm, a bandaged hand, even a scraped knee on a child at the grocery store—any visible injury would trigger the same cascade, his brain insisting that violence was imminent, that he was in danger. These moments would come without warning. Marcus could be sitting at his desk, focused on a color palette, when an intrusive thought would arrive fully formed: the memory of the officer's grip, the smell of the patrol car's interior, the sensation of his cheekbone against cold metal. His body would respond instantly, heart racing, muscles coiling as though he needed to run.

What frightened Marcus most was that he had come to believe his life was fundamentally destroyed. The man who had been tackled on that roadside was not the man he had been before; that version had been erased. He was certain now that nothing mattered—his work felt hollow, his marriage felt fragile, his sense of safety had been revealed as an illusion. Nothing he did seemed to change the fact that the world had shown itself to be unjust and cruel. An officer had assaulted him without cause, and nothing had come of it—no accountability, no apology that meant anything. The injustice of it sat in his chest like a stone, and with it came a conviction that his life would never recover. These dark certainties fed a constant vigilance: Marcus found himself unable to relax even at home, unable to sit in a restaurant without mentally mapping the exits, unable to feel his body as anything other than a taut instrument braced against the next blow.

When the memories returned—unbidden, overwhelming—Marcus would feel such a surge of emotion that he would have to stop whatever he was doing. The sensation was not merely recollection; it was re-living. He would be back on that roadside, the fear as fresh as it had been that night, and the only way he knew to survive it was to escape into his phone. He had begun spending hours scrolling through games, news, anything to keep his mind occupied and away from the memory itself. The distraction worked, briefly. But it was a cycle: the mental occupation would prevent him from processing what had happened, so the memory remained sharp and intrusive, waiting to ambush him at unexpected moments. His phone had become both shield and prison. Elena had started to notice his absence, the way he would disappear into the screen rather than speak to her, the way he had begun avoiding friends and colleagues, declining invitations, staying home. The more he isolated himself, the more his mind would circle back to the trauma, and the more desperately he would reach for the phone to push it away again.

The constant mental distraction and avoidance had consequences beyond the digital realm. At work, his creative output had suffered; he had missed deadlines, and his supervisor had begun to question his reliability. His marriage, once warm and easy, had become strained. Elena would ask him what was wrong, and he could not explain it clearly—when he tried to tell her about the incident, the words would scatter, the narrative would break apart, and he would be left stammering, unable to finish, unable to make her understand why he could not simply move past it. His body remained perpetually on alert, muscles tight, sleep fragmented. Even when he forced himself to stay away from his phone, the vigilance would spike; he would scan rooms for threats, identify exits, feel his shoulders creep up toward his ears. The avoidance was supposed to protect him, but it had only deepened the trap. Every time he escaped into distraction, every time he avoided a social situation or a police car on the street, he was reinforcing the message that the world was dangerous and that he could not cope. The threat felt more real, the memories more vivid, the conviction that his life was over more absolute.

Now, three months later, Marcus sat in the waiting room of a therapist's office, his phone face-down on his lap—a small victory, though it cost him. He was here because Elena had finally said that she could not watch him disappear anymore, that something had to change. What Marcus feared most was that no change was possible, that he would spend the rest of his life trapped in this loop of vigilance and escape, watching his marriage crumble, his career falter, his sense of self dissolve into nothing. But beneath that fear, barely audible, was a whisper of hope: that perhaps someone could help him understand why the world had become so dangerous, and whether it might ever feel safe again.
